title: AI compute will be exhausted, but its owners probably won't be
dek: In the last fiber-optic bubble, the most-indebted companies collapsed first, but the fiber assets kept working when others took them over. Mike Volpi believes this GPU buildout will follow the same script: the assets will be fully utilized, but their ownership may well change hands.
why: Mike Volpi led Cisco's acquisitions and network buildout in the 1990s and contrasts the capital structures, asset lifecycles, and M&A logic of the two infrastructure booms from firsthand experience.
who: Investors, founders, and engineers interested in AI infrastructure investment cycles, GPU asset pricing and M&A strategy, and network architecture.
skip: The introduction of Mike Volpi's background and opening remarks (0:00-3:00) can be skipped without losing the main argument.

points.h: Bandwidth jumped by technology breakthroughs; compute is stuck drinking from Moore's Law
points.body: In the 1990s, fiber-optic bandwidth multiplied 40-80x through WDM (wavelength-division multiplexing)—packing multiple colors of light down the same fiber. AI compute expansion is fundamentally different: constrained by Moore's Law, it grows slower. Volpi sees this as the root technical difference between the two buildouts—the pace of supply growth is not even close.

points.h: Assets will be exhausted; their owners will likely not
points.body: Volpi reviews the Internet bubble: companies most burdened by debt collapsed first, but their fiber assets didn't disappear—others picked them up cheap and kept using them. He expects the same script to play out: data centers and chips will be fully utilized, even beyond expectations, but whoever ends up owning these assets may well not be the companies building them today.

points.h: H100s should be obsolete; their rental price keeps rising
points.body: Four years ago, conventional wisdom said H100-class chips had about five years of useful life—and rented for roughly $1.82 per GPU-hour. By all rights they should have cheapened as they neared end-of-life, but instead they now rent for $2.50-3.00 per hour. Volpi attributes this to extreme compute scarcity: as long as semiconductor production lags demand, older chips stay needed, and asset lifecycles stretch far beyond what finance models assumed.

points.h: Cisco's M&A philosophy: accept one-third total loss
points.body: Volpi recalls Cisco's acquisition method: split outcomes roughly into thirds—one-third worked great, one-third was mediocre, one-third failed outright. The company tolerated the failure rate as long as it did it often enough to hit several genuine home runs. Some acquisitions cost $500 million and generated $1 billion in profit within two years. By around 2000, half of Cisco's revenue came from acquired businesses, and no single acquisition ever exceeded 4-5% of the company's market cap.

points.h: NVIDIA's spending on neocloud startups will fail to reshape the market
points.body: On NVIDIA's practice of investing in numerous neocloud companies to cultivate more buyers, Volpi argues it won't change the industry's final shape: in any sector where scale dominates, no amount of money pumped into small players will stop consolidation into a handful of giants—like how US aviation ended with three major carriers. NVIDIA does this not for financial returns but to avoid negotiating with only three or four mega-customers, but it's only delaying, not altering, the industry's natural evolution.

points.h: Model routing emerges as token prices diverge 5-7x
points.body: For the past two years, the market default was to use only the most advanced frontier-model tokens. But Volpi observes the market growing smarter: top-tier Anthropic tokens and top-tier Kimi tokens differ by 5x, even 7x in price—a gap wide enough to spawn a new business called ‘model routers’ that split requests to different-priced models by task difficulty. He sees this making AI's total demand price-sensitive for the first time, instead of blindly chasing the most expensive model.

points.h: Order bubbles burst: Cisco's market cap fell to one-tenth in six months
points.body: Volpi recounts Cisco's collapse: tight delivery windows led customers to habitually over-order to guard against allocation cuts, and Cisco transferred risk to suppliers by paying early to hoard stock. When true demand softened, orders dropped directly to one-quarter of what they'd been. Combined with risk already locked into the supply chain, the company missed 35-40% of quarterly revenue in a single quarter. Stock fell from over $80 to $9, a ninefold decline in six months.

points.h: AI data centers should abandon stat-muxing for deterministic circuits
points.body: Internet-era switch design assumed bursty traffic, using stat-muxing to smooth peaks and valleys. AI data centers run GPUs at full load constantly, with highly predictable, nearly-deterministic traffic—especially in training. Volpi argues that today's mainstream Broadcom Tomahawk stat-muxing architecture is ‘enough bandwidth but wrong shape’—what should exist is a new switching architecture designed for full-time load, needing no buffers. This is classic innovator's dilemma: incumbent vendors won't cannibalize their own business. The opportunity goes to new entrants willing to all-in on the new architecture.
